hypothesis: If Arizona's climate over the past ~500 years fluctuated with a regular ~150-year period, then century-smoothed ring-width chronologies of Arizona Pinus ponderosa will show a statistically significant spectral peak at about 150 years (135-165 yr) that is consistent across sites.
pass_criterion: Use ITRDB Pinus ponderosa chronologies from Arizona that cover at least AD 1500-1950 (at least 5 sites). Detrend each with a conservative spline or negative-exponential fit, build a site-mean index, and apply a 100-year smoother. Run multitaper spectral analysis on the unsmoothed standardized series. The claim passes if (a) the Arizona composite has a spectral peak with period 135-165 yr that exceeds the 95% AR(1) red-noise confidence limit, (b) that peak is the largest peak in the 80-250 yr band, and (c) at least 50% of individual site chronologies show a significant peak in 135-165 yr. The smoothed composite must also show at least 3 successive maxima spaced 150 +/- 20 yr apart.
fail_criterion: The claim fails if the composite has no 135-165 yr peak above the 95% red-noise limit. It also fails if the largest 80-250 yr peak lies outside 135-165 yr, or if fewer than 50% of sites show a significant 135-165 yr peak. It also fails if the smoothed maxima intervals have a coefficient of variation above 0.25, or if fewer than 3 maxima are spaced 150 +/- 20 yr apart.
interpretation: 'Century-smoothed annual ring widths' is read as 100-year running means of standardized ring-width indices, with the spectral analysis done on the unsmoothed series. 'Regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years' is read as a stable, statistically significant spectral peak at 150 yr +/- 10%, together with evenly spaced maxima. 'Climate' is read as the tree-growth signal, which in Arizona is mainly moisture-limited. The moisture-versus-temperature part is not tested. Modern detrending and red-noise significance testing replace Douglass's visual inspection of smoothed curves. Modern ITRDB chronologies are much more numerous than Douglass's original Arizona sample.

dataset.name: International Tree-Ring Data Bank (ITRDB)
dataset.publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), World Data Service for Paleoclimatology
dataset.why_it_fits: The ITRDB holds downloadable ring-width measurement files (.rwl) and standardized chronologies (.crn) with site metadata. I would filter on species code PIPO (Pinus ponderosa), state Arizona, and chronology start year of AD 1500 or earlier. Fields used: year, ring-width index or raw width, sample depth, latitude/longitude and species. The record is long enough (about 3 cycles of 150 yr) to test the claimed period, though only coarsely.
